title: Coexisting posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and ischemic hepatopathy: A case report
case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman with alcohol abuse, intravenous drug use, depression, and untreated hypertension presented after a witnessed generalized tonic–clonic seizure. Earlier that morning she had complained of nausea and vision changes. She was postictal on arrival to the emergency department. Her blood pressure was 170/103 mmHg and heart rate was 104 beats/min; other vital signs were normal. Outpatient records showed chronically elevated pressures of 150–180 s/80–90 s mmHg without antihypertensive therapy. Laboratory tests revealed AST 5,359 IU/L, ALT 2,359 IU/L, total bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 81 IU/L, lactate 18.1 mmol/L, venous pH 7.11, anion gap 31 mmol/L, and WBC 17,800/μL. A urine drug screen and serum alcohol level were negative. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ischemia. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT showed a small left parietal scalp swelling without fracture. Right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrated a normal liver and gallbladder. Lumbar puncture was unremarkable. The patient was admitted, and the initial differential diagnosis included alcohol withdrawal, hepatic encephalopathy, infection, or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.  
By hospital day 1 her mentation normalized, lactate fell to 5.5 mmol/L, pH rose to 7.44, and AST/ALT began to decline. She never exhibited signs of alcohol withdrawal. Additional hepatic studies showed ferritin 16,368 ng/mL, iron 289 µg/dL, transferrin saturation 98%, and negative markers for hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV. Tests for hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, and autoimmune hepatitis were negative. Neurology and hepatology were consulted; neurology recommended a brain MRI, and hepatology suggested ischemic hepatopathy secondary to seizure activity.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Alcohol withdrawal was considered because of her alcohol‐use history but was excluded — “Patient was placed on the alcohol withdrawal management protocol per the institution’s policy but did not show any signs of alcohol withdrawal throughout the 6‐day admission.”  
2. Hepatic encephalopathy was considered given the transaminitis and altered mental status but was excluded — “…neither there was no history of long‐standing liver dysfunction or hepatitis nor was there evidence of hepatic encephalopathy or hyperammonemia.”  
3. Central nervous system infection was considered because of seizure but was excluded — “Lumbar puncture was unremarkable without evidence of central nervous system infection.”  
4. Viral hepatitis was excluded by serologies — “Viral hepatitis markers (hepatitis A/B/C, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein‐Barr virus) were negative.”  
5. Genetic and autoimmune liver diseases were excluded — “Studies for hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, and autoimmune hepatitis were also negative.”  
6. Acetaminophen‐induced hepatic injury was considered but deemed unlikely — “less likely given that the liver enzymes continued to improve with optimized BP control even with continued administration of hydrocodone‐acetaminophen as needed for pain.”  
7. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome was confirmed by characteristic MRI findings — “These findings were consistent with PRES.”
